title: Why does heartbreak hurt so much?
description_html:
Anyone who has had their heart broken will know how horrible it feels. But did you know that the pain you feel is not just imaginary – it registers in the same part of the brain that processes physical pain. So, why do we feel this pain? And if it feels so bad, what is the point of being in love in the first place? Neil and Georgie discuss this and teach you some new vocabulary.

6 Minute English now has a VIDEO VERSION! 6 Minute English now comes with a video! It's the same programme that you know and love, but now you can see us! Watch this podcast here (and find a free worksheet): https://www.bbc.co.uk/learningenglish/english/features/6-minute-english_2026/ep-261001 Let us know what you think of the new version of 6 Minute English at learningenglish@bbc.co.uk

cues.t: Hi Georgie.
Hi Neil.
Now, I want you to think back to the last time you had your heart broken.
How did it feel?
It was a couple of years ago.
And I just remember a really intense, sad emotion.
But it also sometimes feels like a physical pain in your stomach, doesn't it?
It does.
It's like real pain, isn't it?
And today, in 6 Minute English, we're talking about heartbreak.
Now, heartbreak is the feeling of sadness we get when we lose someone we love.
And that pain you feel, it's not just imaginary.
In this podcast, we'll be understanding how our brains change when we fall in love and asking the question, why does heartbreak hurt so much?
And as usual, we'll be learning some useful new vocabulary.
You can find the full list and the definitions at bbclearningenglish.com.
Georgie, we're going to start with a quiz question.
Are you ready?
I am very ready.
So, in the 1950s, psychologists noticed a link between children's early bonds with their parents and their romantic relationships as adults, but what is this theory called?
Is it: a) contraction theory, b) attachment theory, or c) superstition theory?
I think it's b) attachment theory.
OK.
Well, we will find out at the end of the programme.
What's going on in our brains when we fall in love?
Well, scientists have scanned people's brains while they're looking at a photo of their romantic partner.
And they found that looking at someone you're in love with activates a part of the brain that also reminds us to eat and drink.
And do scientists know why being in love impacts our brain in this way?
So, it's all about survival.
Our brains have evolved to be this way.
Dr Lucy Brown explains more to the BBC World Service.
This is a survival system.
Nature gave us these systems to be addicted to each other – for reproduction, for protection.
You're oriented completely toward the other person.
It's like hunger or thirst.
Lucy says our brains make us addicted to our romantic partners.
If you're addicted to something, you want more of it.
You can literally be addicted to things like drugs or alcohol, but we also use it metaphorically to talk about things we love.
She says that romantic partners are oriented to each other, which in British English we say orientated, and it means they are pointed towards each other.
They think of each other before other people.
Neil, is there anything else scientists have discovered from scanning the brains of people in love?
Well, being in love doesn't just change the way we think.
It changes our whole identity.
A 2013 study showed us more about this.
People were shown statements about themselves – for example, Neil is kind – and the part of the brain we use to think about ourselves lit up.
When showing the same statements about their partner, the same part of the brain was active – not the part of the brain we generally use to think about others.
So, Neil, are all of these brain changes that come with being in love actually good for us?
Well, studies suggest that good social connections help manage stress and support our immune system.
Professor Zoe Donaldson explained more to the BBC World Service.
Having really strong social bonds increases your likelihood that you'll survive from just about anything, whether that be cancer, depression, etc.
And it overall is the number one predictor of longevity.
So, if you are lonely and you don't have bonds, then your mortality risk goes up in a way that's equivalent to being obese or smoking.
So, having strong social bonds or close relationships with other people makes you more likely to survive disease, according to Zoe.
Yes, it's an important factor in our longevity, which means how long we live.
In fact, Zoe says, being lonely and not having good social bonds increases your mortality risk, your risk of dying, by as much as being obese or smoking.
OK.
So, what happens when these bonds are broken, when we experience heartbreak?
Well, scientists have been looking at this by asking people to look at photos of their exes, their former partners, and scanning their brains.
They found that heartbreak activates parts of the brain we use when we're in danger or in pain.
Professor Zoe Donaldson explains more.
It's literal pain in your brain.

So, if you look at the parts of the brain that light up, they overlap with the same brain regions that are activated when you feel visceral pain – when you feel actual, you know... like you get a burn, or you break a... you break a bone.
OK.
So, now it's time for the answer to the quiz question I asked you.
It was about a theory developed by psychologists in the 1950s, which says that children's early relationships with their parents impact their relationships as adults.
What's the name of the theory?
I was quite confident about this, wasn't I, Neil?
I said attachment theory.
Well, you had a reason to be confident because you are correct.
Yay! OK.
Let's recap the vocabulary we learnt in this programme, starting with heartbreak, which is the feeling you experience after you lose someone you love.
If you're addicted to someone or something, you want more of it all the time.
Oriented or orientated towards is used metaphorically to mean that someone or something is your main focus.
Social bonds are the close relationships we have with family, friends and romantic partners.
Longevity means how long you'll live.
And an ex is a past romantic partner that you are no longer in a relationship with.
Once again, our six minutes are up, but you can test what you've learned with the worksheet on our website.
Go to bbclearningenglish.com.
Thanks for joining us and goodbye.
Goodbye.

study.one_liner_ko: 실연의 고통은 상상이 아니라, 사랑에 빠진 뇌가 생존 시스템으로 작동하기 때문에 실제 신체적 통증처럼 느껴진다는 이야기.
summary_ko: 실연(heartbreak)은 사랑하는 사람을 잃었을 때 느끼는 슬픔이다. 위장이 아픈 것처럼 실제 신체 통증으로 느껴지기도 하며, 이 고통은 상상이 아니다.
연인의 사진을 볼 때 뇌에서는 먹고 마시도록 상기시키는 영역이 활성화된다. 사랑은 생식과 보호를 위한 '생존 시스템'이라서 배고픔이나 갈증처럼 작동한다는 것이 Lucy Brown 박사의 설명이다.
사랑은 사고방식만이 아니라 정체성도 바꾼다. 2013년 연구에서 자신에 관한 문장과 연인에 관한 문장을 볼 때 뇌의 같은 영역이 활성화되었다.
Zoe Donaldson 교수에 따르면 강한 사회적 유대는 장수의 가장 강력한 예측 변수다. 외로움이 사망 위험을 높이는 정도는 비만이나 흡연에 맞먹는다.
전 연인의 사진을 보며 뇌를 스캔하면, 위험이나 통증에 반응하는 영역이 켜진다. 화상을 입거나 뼈가 부러질 때 활성화되는 영역과 겹쳐서 '뇌 속의 실제 통증'이라고 할 수 있다.
퀴즈 정답은 attachment theory(애착 이론)다. 마지막에 heartbreak, addicted, oriented, social bonds, longevity, ex를 복습한다.
study.summary_en: This week's episode asks why heartbreak hurts so much. The short answer is that the pain isn't imaginary. When people look at a photo of their partner, a part of the brain linked to hunger and thirst lights up, because love works like a survival system. It even changes our sense of identity. Strong social bonds are also one of the best predictors of how long we live, and loneliness raises your mortality risk about as much as smoking. So when a relationship ends, the brain regions that react to physical pain, like a burn or a broken bone, switch on too. It's literally pain in your brain.

expressions.quote: think back to the last time you had your heart broken
expressions.nuance_ko: 상대를 과거의 기억 속으로 데려가는 도입 표현이다. 발표나 인터뷰에서 청중이 직접 경험을 떠올리게 할 때 효과적이다. 'remember'보다 시간을 거슬러 가는 느낌이 있고, 뒤에 'to + 시점/사건'이 온다.
examples: Think back to your first day at this company. What worried you the most?
When I think back to that trip, the thing I remember is the food.
Let's think back to 2020 for a second, because that's where this whole trend started.

similar.example: Cast your mind back to last winter, when the trains were constantly delayed.
I look back on those years with mixed feelings.

expressions.nuance_ko: 복잡한 현상을 한 가지 핵심 원인으로 정리할 때 쓰는 구어체 표현이다. 논점을 선명하게 만들지만 단정적으로 들릴 수 있다. 격식 있는 자리에서는 'at its core, it's about ~'가 무난하다.
examples: Honestly, a good interview is all about preparation.
With hotels, it's all about location. Everything else is secondary.
Don't overthink it. Negotiation is all about listening.

similar.example: In the end, it comes down to whether you trust the team.

similar.expression: at the end of the day
similar.example: At the end of the day, people just want to feel heard.

expressions.quote: the part of the brain we use to think about ourselves lit up
expressions.nuance_ko: 뇌 스캔에서 영역이 활성화되는 것을 비유적으로 말한다. 일상에서는 'her face lit up'처럼 표정이 밝아지는 의미로도 쓴다. 과거형은 lit이다.
examples: Her whole face lit up when she saw her old teacher.
My phone lit up with messages the second the news broke.
Mention football and his eyes light up.

similar.example: Certain areas of the brain get activated when we hear music we love.
She perked up as soon as coffee was mentioned.

expressions.quote: being in love doesn't just change the way we think. It changes our whole identity
expressions.nuance_ko: 'It's not just X, it's Y' 계열의 논점 확장 패턴이다. 앞 문장은 흔한 생각, 뒤 문장은 더 큰 주장이라서 패널이나 회의에서 힘 있게 말할 때 좋다. 뒤 문장에 whole, entire 같은 강조어를 붙이면 더 강해진다.
examples: Remote work doesn't just save commuting time. It changes how people think about where to live.
A bad manager doesn't just slow a team down. They drive the best people out.
Travelling alone doesn't just give you freedom. It forces you to talk to strangers.

similar.expression: it's not just X, it's Y
similar.example: It's not just a pay issue, it's a respect issue.
The film is not only funny but also quite moving.

expressions.quote: you'll survive from just about anything
expressions.nuance_ko: 'just about'은 '거의'라는 뜻이라서 'almost anything'보다 편하고 구어적이다. just about everyone, just about done처럼 확장해서 쓴다. 과장을 약하게 완화하는 효과도 있다.
examples: My sister can fix just about anything with a bit of tape.
You can find just about anything at that flea market.
I'm just about ready. Give me two minutes.

similar.example: He'll eat pretty much anything you put in front of him.
You can book almost anything online these days.

expressions.quote: your mortality risk goes up in a way that's equivalent to being obese
expressions.nuance_ko: risk goes up/rises/increases 중 goes up이 가장 구어적이다. 'in a way that's equivalent to ~'로 크기를 익숙한 대상에 비교하면 숫자 없이도 설득력이 생긴다. 반대는 risk goes down/drops.
examples: If you skip sleep for weeks, your risk of burnout goes up a lot.
Your risk of getting scammed goes up in a way that's comparable to clicking every link in your inbox.
The risk of missing the flight goes up if you leave it that late.

similar.example: Working nights can raise the risk of heart problems.
The danger is on a par with driving without a seatbelt.

expressions.quote: the number one predictor of longevity
expressions.nuance_ko: 'the number one X of Y' 구조는 1위 요인을 못 박는 표현이라 인상적이다. 데이터나 연구 맥락에서 자주 쓰며, 상관관계를 말할 뿐 인과를 증명하는 것은 아니다. 'a strong predictor of'로 톤을 낮출 수 있다.
examples: Past behaviour is usually the best predictor of future behaviour.
Her coach says attitude is the number one predictor of success in the team.
Honestly, a quiet first week is a poor predictor of how the job will go.

similar.example: How people treat waiters is a good indicator of their character.
Constant lateness is a telling sign of disorganisation.

expressions.expression: a link between X and Y
expressions.quote: noticed a link between children's early bonds with their parents
expressions.nuance_ko: 인과를 단정하지 않고 연관성만 짚을 때 안전한 표현이다. notice/find/establish/suggest a link between ~ 형태로 쓴다. 인과를 말하고 싶으면 'cause', 'drive'를 쓴다.
examples: Researchers found a link between poor sleep and low mood.
I don't see a link between the two incidents.
There's a clear link between how people commute and how they feel at work.

similar.example: Higher screen time is correlated with shorter attention spans.
Her mood seems tied to the weather.

expressions.quote: they overlap with the same brain regions that are activated
expressions.nuance_ko: 범위나 영역, 역할이 부분적으로 겹칠 때 쓴다. 팀 업무나 일정에도 자연스럽다. 완전히 같지는 않고 일부가 같다는 뉘앙스이며, 겹치는 일정은 'clash with'를 쓴다.
examples: Our responsibilities overlap with the marketing team's quite a bit.
My holiday overlaps with the conference by two days.
The two novels overlap with each other in surprising ways.

similar.example: Her research intersects with several other fields.
The meeting clashes with my dentist appointment.

expressions.quote: we also use it metaphorically to talk about things we love
expressions.nuance_ko: 단어의 literal(문자 그대로)과 metaphorical(비유적)을 구분해서 설명하는 방식이다. 토론에서 상대가 말을 문자 그대로 받아들일 때 'I mean that metaphorically'라고 정리할 수 있다. 'We use X to talk about Y' 구조도 함께 익혀 두면 좋다.
examples: When I say my inbox is a jungle, I'm using it metaphorically.
People use 'starving' metaphorically all the time, even right after lunch.
He said it metaphorically, but the audience took it literally.

similar.example: Figuratively speaking, we're all in the same boat.
She's my right hand, in a manner of speaking.

expressions.quote: Let's recap the vocabulary we learnt in this programme
expressions.nuance_ko: 회의나 발표의 마무리, 또는 긴 논의 후에 요점을 되짚는 신호다. recap은 동사와 명사 둘 다로 쓴다. 'Let me quickly recap'이 가장 자연스럽다.
examples: Before we wrap up, let me quickly recap what we agreed on.
Let's recap: you book the venue, I'll handle the invitations.
Can you recap the last ten minutes? I got pulled into a call.

similar.example: To sum up, we need more time and a clearer brief.
Just to be clear, nobody is blaming you.

expressions.nuance_ko: 'time is up'의 구체적 변형으로, 시간 길이를 넣어 센스 있게 마무리한다. 진행자나 사회자가 패널을 끝낼 때도 자주 쓴다. 'time's up'은 데드라인이 지났다는 뉘앙스도 있어서 상황에 맞춰 쓴다.
examples: I'd love to keep going, but our hour is up.
Okay, your five minutes are up. Let's hear from the next speaker.
Time's up, everyone. Pens down.

similar.example: We're out of time, so let's pick this up on Thursday.

similar.expression: that's all we have time for
similar.example: That's all we have time for today. Thanks for joining us.

vocab.example: He never really got over the heartbreak of that breakup.
I'm completely addicted to this new crime series.
She's very goal-oriented, so she plans everything weeks ahead.
Moving abroad made me realise how much I value my social bonds back home.
People in that village are famous for their longevity.
A scare like that really makes you think about your own mortality.
I had a visceral reaction to the smell of that old kitchen.
I bumped into my ex at the airport, which was awkward.

warmup.q: Have you ever felt something emotional as a physical sensation, like a knot in your stomach? What was the situation?
warmup.hint_ko: 구체적인 상황(면접, 이별, 발표 등)과 신체 반응을 묘사하고, 어떻게 가라앉혔는지도 말해 보기.

warmup.q: Who in your life would you say you have the strongest social bonds with, and how do you keep them strong from abroad?
warmup.hint_ko: 가족, 친구 등 대상을 정하고 연락 방식, 시차, 만남의 빈도 등 구체적인 습관으로 설명하기.

opinion.q: The episode says loneliness raises mortality risk about as much as smoking. Does that surprise you, and should it change how we think about work and city life?
opinion.hint_ko: 놀라움 여부를 먼저 말하고, 재택근무, 도시의 고립, 해외 생활 등 현대 생활과 연결. 연구가 상관관계에 그칠 수 있다는 점도 언급 가능.

opinion.q: If heartbreak is 'literal pain in your brain', should workplaces and schools take emotional pain more seriously?
opinion.hint_ko: 정신 건강 휴가, 상담 지원 등 구체적 제도를 예로 들고, 개인 영역과 조직의 책임 사이 균형 짚기.

debate.q: Is falling in love worth it, given how much it can hurt when it ends?
debate.for: Love is part of a survival system that also improves health, identity and longevity. Pain is the price of connection, and a life without bonds is riskier.
debate.against: If heartbreak registers like physical injury, deliberately risking it looks irrational. People can build meaningful lives with friends, work and community without a romantic attachment.

roleplay.scenario: You are a guest on a podcast panel about wellbeing. The host asks why breakups hurt so much and whether strong relationships really make us healthier.
roleplay.your_role: Panel guest who has read the research and wants to explain it clearly to a general audience
roleplay.partner_role: Curious, slightly sceptical podcast host who pushes back on the claims
goals: Use at least three expressions from the episode, such as 'it's all about', 'a link between', 'doesn't just ~, it ~'.
Explain the brain-scan findings in your own words, including the overlap with physical pain.
Respond to the host's pushback by distinguishing correlation from causation, then wrap up with 'Let's recap'.

useful_phrases.phrase: It's not just in your head.
useful_phrases.ko: 그건 네 상상이 아니야, 실제로 있는 일이야.

useful_phrases.phrase: That's a fair point, but there's a link worth noting.
useful_phrases.ko: 맞는 말이지만, 짚어 볼 연관성이 있어.

useful_phrases.phrase: It doesn't just affect X, it affects Y.

shadowing.reason_ko: 개인 경험을 말하며 'doesn't it?' 부가의문문으로 공감을 끌어내는 자연스러운 대화 리듬을 익히기 좋다.
'doesn't just ~, it ~' 확장 패턴과 연구 결과를 예시(for example)와 함께 설명하는 흐름을 연습하기에 좋다.
질문으로 다음 논점으로 넘어가는 진행자식 전환 표현이다. 패널이나 회의에서 그대로 응용할 수 있다.

difficulty.note_ko: BBC 6 Minute English 특유의 느리고 또렷한 대본형 진행이라 청취 난도는 낮다. C1 학습자에게는 어휘보다 '연구 결과를 쉽게 풀어 설명하는 구조'와 '증거를 비교해 위험을 말하는 표현'을 가져가는 용도로 적합하다. B1~B2 학습자에게는 어휘 복습과 따라 말하기용으로 이상적이다.

translations.s3: 자, 마지막으로 실연당했을 때를 한번 떠올려 보세요. 기분이 어땠나요?
translations.s4: 몇 년 전이었어요. 아주 강렬하고 슬픈 감정이 있었던 게 기억나요. 그런데 가끔은 배에 실제 통증이 느껴지는 것 같기도 하잖아요, 그렇죠?
translations.s5: 맞아요. 진짜 통증 같죠? 그리고 오늘 6 Minute English에서는 실연에 대해 이야기해 볼 거예요. 실연이란 사랑하는 사람을 잃었을 때 느끼는 슬픔을 말해요. 그리고 그때 느끼는 아픔은 단지 상상이 아니에요. 이번 팟캐스트에서는 사랑에 빠질 때 우리 뇌가 어떻게 변하는지 알아보고, 왜 실연은 그렇게 아픈지 질문해 볼 거예요.
translations.s6: 그리고 늘 그렇듯 유용한 새 어휘도 배워 볼 거예요. 전체 목록과 정의는 bbclearningenglish.com에서 확인하실 수 있어요.
translations.s7: 조지, 퀴즈 문제로 시작해 볼게요. 준비됐어요?
translations.s9: 1950년대에 심리학자들은 아이들이 부모와 맺는 초기 유대와 성인이 되어서의 연애 관계 사이에 연관성이 있다는 걸 알아챘는데요, 이 이론을 뭐라고 부를까요? a) 수축 이론, b) 애착 이론, c) 미신 이론 중에서요.
translations.s11: 좋아요. 정답은 프로그램 끝에서 알려 드릴게요.
translations.s12: 사랑에 빠지면 우리 뇌에서는 무슨 일이 벌어질까요?
translations.s13: 과학자들이 사람들에게 연인의 사진을 보여 주면서 뇌를 스캔해 봤어요. 그랬더니 사랑하는 사람을 바라볼 때, 먹고 마시라고 알려 주는 뇌 영역도 함께 활성화된다는 걸 발견했죠.
translations.s14: 그럼 과학자들은 사랑이 왜 이런 식으로 뇌에 영향을 주는지 알고 있나요?
translations.s15: 다 생존과 관련이 있어요. 우리 뇌가 그렇게 진화한 거죠. 루시 브라운 박사가 BBC 월드 서비스에서 더 자세히 설명해 줍니다.
translations.s16: 이건 생존 시스템이에요. 자연은 우리가 서로에게 중독되도록 이런 시스템을 줬어요. 번식과 보호를 위해서요. 우리는 완전히 상대방을 향하게 돼요. 배고픔이나 갈증 같은 거예요.
translations.s17: 루시는 우리 뇌가 연인에게 중독되게 만든다고 말해요. 어떤 것에 중독되면 그걸 더 원하게 되죠. 약물이나 술 같은 것에 말 그대로 중독될 수도 있지만, 우리가 사랑하는 것들을 이야기할 때도 비유적으로 이 말을 써요.
translations.s18: 그리고 루시는 연인들이 서로에게 oriented되어 있다고 말하는데, 영국 영어로는 orientated라고 해요. 서로를 향해 있다는 뜻이에요. 다른 사람들보다 서로를 먼저 생각한다는 거죠.
translations.s19: 닐, 사랑에 빠진 사람들의 뇌를 스캔해서 과학자들이 알아낸 게 또 있나요?
translations.s20: 사랑에 빠지면 생각하는 방식만 달라지는 게 아니에요. 우리의 정체성 전체가 바뀌어요. 2013년의 한 연구가 이에 대해 더 많은 걸 보여 줬죠. 사람들에게 자기 자신에 대한 문장, 예를 들면 '닐은 친절하다' 같은 걸 보여 줬더니, 자신에 대해 생각할 때 쓰는 뇌 영역이 활성화됐어요. 그런데 파트너에 대한 같은 문장을 보여 줬을 때도 같은 영역이 활성화됐어요. 보통 다른 사람에 대해 생각할 때 쓰는 영역이 아니라요.
translations.s21: 그럼 닐, 사랑에 빠지면서 일어나는 이런 뇌의 변화가 실제로 우리에게 다 좋은 건가요?
translations.s22: 연구들에 따르면 좋은 사회적 관계는 스트레스를 관리하고 면역 체계를 돕는다고 해요. 조이 도널드슨 교수가 BBC 월드 서비스에서 더 자세히 설명했어요.
translations.s23: 정말 강한 사회적 유대가 있으면 암이든 우울증이든 거의 어떤 것에서도 살아남을 가능성이 높아져요. 그리고 전반적으로 수명을 예측하는 가장 중요한 요인이기도 해요. 그래서 외롭고 유대가 없다면 사망 위험이 비만이나 흡연과 맞먹을 만큼 올라가요.
translations.s24: 그러니까 조이에 따르면, 강한 사회적 유대나 다른 사람들과의 가까운 관계가 있으면 병에서 살아남을 가능성이 더 높아진다는 거네요.
translations.s25: 네, 그건 longevity, 즉 얼마나 오래 사느냐에 중요한 요인이에요. 실제로 조이는 외롭고 좋은 사회적 유대가 없으면 사망 위험, 그러니까 죽을 위험이 비만이나 흡연만큼 높아진다고 말해요.
translations.s26: 좋아요. 그럼 이런 유대가 끊어지면, 그러니까 실연을 겪으면 어떻게 될까요?
translations.s27: 과학자들은 사람들에게 전 연인, 그러니까 예전 파트너의 사진을 보게 하고 뇌를 스캔해서 이걸 살펴봤어요. 그랬더니 실연이 위험에 처했을 때나 고통스러울 때 쓰는 뇌 영역을 활성화한다는 걸 발견했죠. 조이 도널드슨 교수가 더 자세히 설명해 줍니다.
translations.s28: 그건 말 그대로 뇌 속의 통증이에요. 활성화되는 뇌 영역을 보면, 실제 신체적 통증을 느낄 때, 그러니까 화상을 입거나 뼈가 부러졌을 때 활성화되는 뇌 영역과 겹쳐요.
translations.s29: 자, 이제 제가 낸 퀴즈의 정답을 알려 드릴 시간이에요. 1950년대에 심리학자들이 발전시킨 이론에 관한 문제였죠. 아이들이 부모와 맺는 초기 관계가 성인이 되었을 때의 관계에 영향을 준다는 이론인데요. 이 이론의 이름이 뭘까요?
translations.s30: 저는 꽤 자신 있었잖아요, 그렇죠, 닐? 애착 이론이라고 했죠.
translations.s32: 야호! 좋아요. 이번 프로그램에서 배운 어휘를 정리해 볼게요. 먼저 heartbreak, 사랑하는 사람을 잃은 뒤에 겪는 감정이에요.
translations.s33: 누군가나 무언가에 addicted되어 있다면, 그걸 항상 더 원한다는 뜻이에요.
translations.s34: Oriented 또는 orientated towards는 비유적으로 쓰여서, 어떤 사람이나 대상이 내 주된 관심사라는 뜻이에요.
translations.s35: Social bonds는 가족, 친구, 연인과 맺는 가까운 관계를 말해요.
translations.s37: 그리고 ex는 더 이상 사귀지 않는 과거의 연인을 말해요.
translations.s38: 이번에도 6분이 다 지났네요. 하지만 웹사이트의 워크시트로 배운 내용을 확인해 보실 수 있어요. bbclearningenglish.com으로 가 보세요.
